result.summary: Mercury steals Apollo's cattle at Pylos while Apollo is distracted by love and his pipe. The old herdsman Battus sees him and accepts a cow to keep silent. Mercury returns in disguise, tests him with a bigger bribe, and turns him into a touchstone when he talks.

scenes.title: Argument and Apollo's absence
scenes.summary: The prose summary gives the outline of the fable, then the poet notes that Apollo could not help Chiron and was away in Elis and Messenia.

scenes.title: Apollo as shepherd; cattle stolen
scenes.summary: Apollo, dressed as a shepherd and in love, plays his pipe while Mercury drives his cows into the woods. Only the old herdsman Battus sees it.
scenes.stakes: Apollo's herd is lost through his distraction; Mercury risks discovery.

scenes.title: Mercury bribes Battus
scenes.summary: Mercury gives Battus a cow to deny seeing the herd. Battus promises silence, saying a stone would sooner tell.
scenes.stakes: Mercury risks exposure of the theft.

scenes.title: Disguised test and the touchstone
scenes.summary: Mercury returns in disguise and offers a cow and bull. Battus betrays the secret, and Mercury turns him into a touchstone.
scenes.stakes: Battus loses his human form as punishment for perjury.

alias_notes.explanation: Chiron was the son of the nymph Philyra.

notable_quotes.reason: Mercury's ironic rebuke of Battus for betraying him to himself.

analysis.text: The tale punishes broken promises and greed: Battus can be bought twice and pays by being turned to stone.
The story gives an origin for the touchstone, used to test the purity of gold, as Battus's loyalty is tested.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's tale echoes the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, where the infant Hermes steals Apollo's cattle.

language_notes.text: The Philyrean hero is the centaur Chiron, son of Philyra. He was wounded and in agony, and Apollo, god of healing, could not cure him.
The translator's braces mark words supplied for sense, such as {God}. Delphi is Apollo's oracle site, and the poet addresses him directly as 'thou'.
Pylos was the city of Neleus in Messenia. The cows are Apollo's, left unguarded while he is distracted by love.
The son of Maia is Mercury (the Greek Hermes), known as a god of thieves and tricks. Here he steals Apollo's cattle.
'Lest no requital be paid thee' means roughly 'so that you are not left unrewarded'. The wording is stiff and archaic.
A touchstone is a dark stone used to test the purity of gold or silver by the streak it leaves. Here it also suggests testing Battus's honesty.

context_notes.text: The pipe with seven reeds of unequal length is the syrinx or panpipe, the shepherd's instrument. Apollo plays it while in disguise.
Neleus was the king of Pylos and father of Nestor. Battus tends his herds and mares.

literary_notes.text: The poet turns to address Apollo directly, giving the narration a tone of sorrowful intimacy.
Battus's boast that a stone would speak sooner than he will be ironically undone, since he himself becomes a stone.
Battus is bought twice, and the insistence that the cows really were there stresses that his betrayal was true, not a guess.
The tale ends by explaining the origin of the name 'touchstone', a common Ovidian closing for a transformation story.
